why_how.text: Drivers under eighteen reach a full license only through graduated steps that build experience.
The learner permit has its own age, holding period, supervisor rule and curfew.

scenario.text: Kai, fifteen, has had his learner permit for four months and wants to drive alone to a friend's house at nine p.m.

reasoning.text: A permit holder may drive only with a licensed driver twenty-one or older in the front seat, and must hold the permit one hundred eighty days before moving up.

result.text: Kai may not drive alone; he needs a licensed adult of twenty-one or older beside him.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a permit holder may drive alone during daylight.

correction.text: A permit holder may drive only when a licensed driver aged twenty-one or older rides in the front seat, at any hour.

memory_support.text: Permit: fifteen to start, twenty-one beside you, home by ten.

prompt.text: A permit holder wants to drive home from practice at ten thirty p.m. with a licensed parent beside her. Is that allowed?

answer.text: No. A permit holder may not drive between ten p.m. and six a.m.

rationale.text: The curfew applies even with a qualified supervisor in the front seat.

title.text: Four steps to a full license

lines.text: Learner Permit.
Intermediate Restricted, then Unrestricted.
Regular Driver License.

narration.text: Tennessee requires drivers under eighteen to build driving experience through graduated steps before they can hold a full, unrestricted license. The four steps of the Graduated Driver License program are the Learner Permit, the Intermediate Restricted License, the Intermediate Unrestricted License and the Regular Driver License. A license issued at any of the first three steps shows GDL printed in its bottom left corner. This lesson starts at the first step, the learner permit, and covers its requirements, its limits and the penalty for collecting points.

lines.text: Age fifteen.
Written exams and vision screening.
Issued for twelve months.

narration.text: A learner permit requires being fifteen and passing the standard written exams and the vision screening. The GDL review table shows a learner permit issued for twelve months, with a fee of ten dollars and fifty cents for any applicant under eighteen. Learner permit holders and Intermediate Restricted holders each receive a Restriction Card to carry, which explains their limits and what is needed to advance to the next level. Keep that card with you, because it summarizes the rules covered in the rest of this lesson.

lines.text: Licensed driver aged twenty-one or older.
Seated in the front seat.

narration.text: A permit holder may drive only when a licensed driver aged twenty-one or older rides in the front seat. Both parts of that rule must be met every time. A licensed eighteen-year-old does not meet the age requirement, and a qualifying adult in the back seat does not meet the seat requirement. The supervisor rule applies at every hour the permit holder drives, not only at night. So think of the permit as permission to practice beside a qualified adult, and never as permission to drive on your own. Both conditions, every drive.

lines.text: No driving from ten p.m. to six a.m.
Applies even with a supervisor.

narration.text: Here is a trap. A permit holder may not drive between ten p.m. and six a.m., and that curfew applies even when a licensed adult of twenty-one or older is sitting in the front seat. Many learners assume a qualified supervisor makes any hour acceptable, but the permit rules list the curfew separately from the supervisor rule. So a permit holder finishing practice at ten thirty at night must let someone else drive home. Later you will see that the Intermediate Restricted curfew starts an hour later, which is easy to mix up.

lines.text: Hold it one hundred eighty days.
Six points restart the clock.

narration.text: A teen must hold the learner permit for one hundred eighty days before moving up to the Intermediate Restricted License. Points can lengthen that wait. A learner permit holder whose record reaches six or more points must keep the permit until the record stays under six points for one hundred eighty consecutive days. So a permit holder who collects points does not simply finish the original holding period. The clock that matters becomes one hundred eighty consecutive days with fewer than six points, which can push the next step well into the future.

lines.text: Ten thirty p.m. with a parent: allowed?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a permit holder finishes practice at ten thirty at night, and her licensed mother, who is over twenty-one, is sitting beside her. May she drive home? Work it out before reading on. No. A permit holder may not drive between ten p.m. and six a.m. The supervisor rule is met, because a licensed driver aged twenty-one or older is in the front seat, but the curfew is a separate limit. Her mother should drive home, and the permit holder can practice again after six in the morning or earlier in the evening.

lines.text: Fifteen, written and vision tests.
Twenty-one beside you; curfew at ten.
One hundred eighty days, under six points.

narration.text: To wrap up, the GDL has four steps, and licenses at the first three show GDL in the bottom left corner. The learner permit starts at fifteen after the written exams and vision screening, lasts twelve months, and comes with a Restriction Card. A permit holder drives only with a licensed driver twenty-one or older in the front seat, never between ten p.m. and six a.m., and holds the permit one hundred eighty days before moving up. Six or more points mean waiting for one hundred eighty consecutive days under six points.

why_how.text: Each intermediate level has its own age, test and time requirements.
Knowing when the regular license is available helps teens and parents plan.

scenario.text: Ana, sixteen, has held her permit for six months and has fifty logged hours, ten at night, certified by her father.

reasoning.text: The Intermediate Restricted License requires being sixteen, passing the road test, and a certified fifty hours of practice with ten at night.

result.text: Ana is ready to take the road test for her Intermediate Restricted License.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the Intermediate Unrestricted step needs another road test.

correction.text: The Intermediate Unrestricted License needs no additional tests; it is refused only after an at-fault accident or two safety belt violations.

memory_support.text: Sixteen and the road test, then seventeen and a year.

prompt.text: A seventeen-year-old has held Intermediate Restricted for one year with a clean record. Does she need another test to move up?

answer.text: No. The Intermediate Unrestricted License needs no additional tests.

rationale.text: Age seventeen and one year on Intermediate Restricted, without an at-fault accident or two belt violations, are what count.

lines.text: Intermediate Restricted at sixteen.
Intermediate Unrestricted at seventeen.
Regular license at eighteen or graduation.

narration.text: This lesson follows a teen from the learner permit through the two intermediate levels to the regular Class D license. Each step has its own requirements. The Intermediate Restricted License comes first, then the Intermediate Unrestricted License, and finally the regular license. Both intermediate levels list the license class as Class D and display Intermediate Driver License in the yellow header bar on the front. Since July first, two thousand eighteen, every license issued to someone under twenty-one has been printed in a vertical format.

lines.text: Age sixteen.
Pass the road test.
Fifty certified hours, ten at night.

narration.text: The Intermediate Restricted License requires being sixteen and passing the driving skills test, also called the road test. A parent, legal guardian or licensed driving instructor must also certify fifty hours of driving practice, ten of them at night, on the Department's certification form. Remember too that the learner permit must have been held for one hundred eighty days first. So the checklist for this step has three parts: age sixteen, the certified fifty hours with ten at night, and a passed road test. All three must be in place.

lines.text: Age seventeen.
One year on Intermediate Restricted.
Two dollar application fee.

narration.text: Moving up to the Intermediate Unrestricted License requires being seventeen and having held the Intermediate Restricted License for one year. The move costs a two dollars application fee after the one-year minimum. It needs no additional tests. The Intermediate Unrestricted level carries no driving restrictions, so no restriction card is issued for it. In other words, at this level the teen still holds an intermediate license, but the passenger limit and curfew of the restricted level no longer apply. That is the whole requirement for this step.

lines.text: An at-fault traffic accident.
Two safety belt violations.
No extra test is needed.

narration.text: The trap here is thinking the Unrestricted step is automatic, or that it needs another test. Neither is right. The Intermediate Unrestricted License is refused after an at-fault traffic accident or two safety belt violations, and it needs no additional tests. So a teen who turns seventeen and has held Intermediate Restricted for a year can still be refused if there was an at-fault accident or two belt violations. Wearing a seat belt and driving carefully during the restricted year directly decide whether the teen moves up.

lines.text: At eighteen, or on graduating or earning a GED.
Keeps the Under twenty-one markings.
Emancipated sixteen-year-olds qualify.

narration.text: A teen can get the regular Class D license at eighteen or on graduating high school or earning a GED, whichever comes first. The license drops the word Intermediate but keeps its Under twenty-one markings. At eighteen, a driver may pay an eight dollars duplicate fee for a license without the word Intermediate, or keep the Intermediate license until the end of its five-year renewal cycle. A sixteen-year-old emancipated by active-duty military service, marriage or court order may also obtain a regular Class D license.

lines.text: Clean year at seventeen: another test?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a seventeen-year-old has held her Intermediate Restricted License for one year, with no at-fault accident and no safety belt violations. Does she need to pass another test to get the Intermediate Unrestricted License? Work it out before reading on. No. The Intermediate Unrestricted License needs no additional tests. She meets the age of seventeen and the one-year holding period, and nothing on her record blocks the move. She pays the two dollar application fee, and the restricted level's limits no longer apply to her.

lines.text: Sixteen, road test and fifty hours.
Seventeen and one restricted year.
Eighteen, a diploma or a GED for regular.

narration.text: To close, Intermediate Restricted requires age sixteen, a passed road test and fifty certified hours with ten at night. Intermediate Unrestricted requires age seventeen and a year on the restricted level, costs two dollars, needs no new test, and is refused after an at-fault accident or two belt violations. The regular Class D comes at eighteen or on graduating or earning a GED, keeping its Under twenty-one markings, and emancipated sixteen-year-olds may qualify early. Both intermediate cards show Class D and a yellow Intermediate Driver License header.

why_how.text: Intermediate Restricted drivers face a passenger limit and a curfew with specific exceptions.
The permit and restricted rules use similar numbers that are easy to confuse.

scenario.text: Leo, sixteen, has an Intermediate Restricted License and wants to drive two school friends home.

reasoning.text: A restricted driver may carry only one other passenger unless a passenger is twenty-one or older with a valid unrestricted license, or the passengers are siblings in the same home and he carries a parent's letter for school trips.

result.text: Leo may take only one friend unless one of the exceptions applies.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the restricted curfew starts at ten p.m. like the permit curfew.

correction.text: A permit holder may not drive from ten p.m. to six a.m., but the Intermediate Restricted curfew runs from eleven p.m. to six a.m.

memory_support.text: Permit home by ten, restricted home by eleven.

prompt.text: An Intermediate Restricted driver wants to drive at ten thirty p.m. with no adult. Is that inside the curfew?

answer.text: No. The restricted curfew runs from eleven p.m. to six a.m., so ten thirty is allowed.

rationale.text: The ten p.m. limit belongs to the permit; the restricted limit starts at eleven.

lines.text: One passenger, with exceptions.
A curfew from eleven to six.

narration.text: The Intermediate Restricted License lets a teen drive alone, but with limits on passengers and hours. This lesson covers those limits and their exceptions, compares them with the learner permit rules, and finishes with seat belts and work zones. An Intermediate Restricted driver may carry only one other passenger unless an exception applies, and may not drive from eleven p.m. to six a.m. unless another exception applies. The exceptions are specific, so it pays to learn them exactly rather than guessing what counts.

lines.text: Only one other passenger.
Unless one passenger is twenty-one plus with an unrestricted license.
Or siblings with a parent's letter for school.

narration.text: An Intermediate Restricted driver may carry only one other passenger, unless a passenger is twenty-one or older with a valid unrestricted license, or the passengers are siblings living in the same home and the driver carries a parent's letter for school trips. So a sixteen-year-old may not fill the car with friends after school. With an adult passenger of twenty-one or older who holds a valid unrestricted license, more passengers may ride, and brothers and sisters from the same home may ride together to school with the letter.

lines.text: No driving eleven p.m. to six a.m.
Exceptions: parent, designated adult, school, work.
Hunting or fishing from four to six a.m.

narration.text: An Intermediate Restricted driver may not drive from eleven p.m. to six a.m. The exceptions are driving with a parent or guardian, with a licensed driver twenty-one or older designated in writing, going to or from a school event or work with written permission, or going hunting or fishing between four a.m. and six a.m. with a valid license. Each exception has its condition. A trip home from work late at night needs written permission, and an early fishing trip is allowed only from four a.m. with a valid hunting or fishing license.

lines.text: Permit curfew: ten p.m. to six a.m.
Restricted curfew: eleven p.m. to six a.m.
Age twenty-one: supervisor or passenger exception.

narration.text: Two pairs of rules look alike. The curfews differ: a learner permit holder may not drive from ten p.m. to six a.m., while an Intermediate Restricted driver is barred from eleven p.m. to six a.m. The age twenty-one also shows up twice. A permit holder needs a licensed driver twenty-one or older in the front seat, while a restricted driver may carry extra passengers when one passenger is twenty-one or older with a valid unrestricted license. Match each rule to its level before you answer any question about hours or passengers.

lines.text: Restricted driver at ten thirty p.m.: allowed?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a sixteen-year-old with an Intermediate Restricted License wants to drive home alone at ten thirty at night. Is that inside the curfew? Work it out before reading on. It is allowed. The Intermediate Restricted curfew runs from eleven p.m. to six a.m., so ten thirty is still before it begins. The ten p.m. start belongs to the learner permit. If the same driver were still out after eleven, one of the listed exceptions, such as a parent in the car or written permission for work, would be needed.

lines.text: Belts for passengers four through seventeen.
Child restraint under four.
Work zones: no tailgating, merge early.

narration.text: Finally, at the permit and both intermediate levels, seat belts are mandatory for every passenger aged four through seventeen, and a child under four must ride in a child restraint device. Teens are also told that most work zone crashes are rear-end collisions, so do not tailgate and slow to the posted work-zone limit. In a work zone, merge early, obey the flaggers, avoid lane changes unless directed, and switch on headlights before entering. Together with the passenger limit and curfews, these rules shape a teen's first months driving alone.

why_how.text: Points, crashes and forged letters can slow a teen's progress or send them back a level.
Phone rules are stricter for permit and intermediate holders than for other drivers.
The same six points carry a different penalty on the permit than on the restricted level.

scenario.text: Mia, on Intermediate Restricted, collects six points from two minor tickets during her first year.

reasoning.text: Six or more points on Intermediate Restricted add ninety days to the one-year minimum.

result.text: Mia must hold Intermediate Restricted for one year and three months in total before moving up.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking teens may use a phone while driving as long as they do not text.

correction.text: Permit and intermediate holders may not use any cell phone, handheld, car phone or other mobile phone, while driving.

memory_support.text: Six points: permit restarts, restricted extends.

prompt.text: A permit holder reaches six points. Does she simply add ninety days to her permit time?

answer.text: No. On a learner permit she must keep the permit until her record stays under six points for one hundred eighty consecutive days.

rationale.text: The ninety-day addition is the Intermediate Restricted penalty, not the permit penalty.

lines.text: Points and crashes.
Forged letters.
Phone violations.

narration.text: This lesson covers the penalties that slow or reverse progress through the GDL. To understand points, start with a simple comparison: six points on the record is roughly the same as two minor traffic citations. On the Intermediate Restricted License, six or more points, contributing to an accident, or a second seatbelt conviction adds ninety days to the one-year minimum, for one year and three months in total. More serious events, such as a forged letter or a fatal accident, cost far more, and phone violations bring penalties of their own.

lines.text: Six points, an accident or a second belt conviction.
Second moving violation: driver education.
Late-reported violation: back ninety days.

narration.text: On the Intermediate Restricted License, six or more points, contributing to an accident, or a second seatbelt conviction adds ninety days to the one-year minimum. A second moving-violation conviction requires finishing a certified driver education course before advancing. And if a violation from the restricted period reaches the Department only after the Unrestricted license is issued, the teen drops back to Intermediate Restricted for ninety days. So a violation can still matter even after the teen has already moved up a level.

lines.text: Forged parental approval letter.
Contributing to a fatal accident.
Only a permit until age eighteen.

narration.text: Some actions erase the restricted license entirely. A forged letter of parental approval, or contributing to a fatal accident, revokes the Intermediate Restricted License and leaves the teen with only a learner permit until age eighteen. Being convicted of carrying a forged or fraudulent permission letter has the same result. These are not delays measured in days; they send the teen back to the first step of the program until eighteen. The permission letters for passengers and curfew exceptions must always be genuine.

lines.text: Permit: one hundred eighty clean days.
Restricted: ninety added days.

narration.text: Here is the trap: the same six points mean different things on different levels. On a learner permit, six or more points restart a wait of one hundred eighty consecutive clean days, while on the Intermediate Restricted License the same points add ninety days to the one-year minimum. So a permit holder with six points must keep the permit until the record stays under six points for one hundred eighty consecutive days. A restricted driver with six points adds ninety days. Always ask which level the driver holds before you work out the penalty.

lines.text: Teens: no cell phone use at all while driving.
Teen conviction: misdemeanor, fine, points, delay.
Everyone: no texting while driving.

narration.text: Tennessee bans any learner permit or intermediate license holder from using a cell phone, whether handheld, car phone or other mobile phone, while driving on a Tennessee road. A teen convicted under the ban faces a Class C misdemeanor, a fifty dollars fine, six points on the record and a ninety-day delay in Intermediate Restricted eligibility. Since July first, two thousand nine, texting while driving has been banned for all drivers, with a fine of no more than fifty dollars plus court costs of no more than ten dollars.

lines.text: Six points on a permit: just ninety days?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a learner permit holder reaches six points. Does she simply add ninety days to her permit time, like a restricted driver would? Work it out before reading on. No. On a learner permit, she must keep the permit until her record stays under six points for one hundred eighty consecutive days. The ninety-day addition belongs to the Intermediate Restricted License, where six or more points add ninety days to the one-year minimum. The level the driver holds decides which penalty applies. Check the level first.

lines.text: Six points: about two minor tickets.
Forgery or a fatal accident: permit until eighteen.
No phones for teens; no texting for anyone.

narration.text: To wrap up, six points equal roughly two minor citations. On a permit they mean one hundred eighty clean days; on Intermediate Restricted, points, an accident or a second belt conviction add ninety days, a second moving violation requires driver education, and a late-reported violation drops the teen back for ninety days. Forged letters or contributing to a fatal accident leave only a permit until eighteen. Teens may not use any cell phone while driving, with heavy penalties, and texting while driving is banned for all drivers.

why_how.text: A teen moving to Tennessee enters the GDL at a level that depends on what they held before.
Out-of-state time can count, but the Tennessee restricted year still applies.

scenario.text: Zoe, sixteen, moves to Tennessee with an out-of-state license issued five months earlier and a clean record.

reasoning.text: A sixteen-year-old with a valid out-of-state license issued at least ninety days before applying applies for the Intermediate Restricted License.

result.text: Zoe applies for Intermediate Restricted and must hold it one year before moving up.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking two years on an out-of-state license skips the Tennessee restricted year.

correction.text: However long a license was held in another state, the Tennessee Intermediate Restricted License must still be held one year before the Unrestricted level.

memory_support.text: Out-of-state time can count, but the Tennessee year stays.

prompt.text: A fifteen-year-old arrives with a valid out-of-state permit. What can she get in Tennessee?

rationale.text: She must reach one hundred eighty total days on a permit and turn sixteen before Intermediate Restricted.

lines.text: Where a newcomer teen enters.
What out-of-state time counts.

narration.text: Teens who move to Tennessee do not start from scratch, but they do join the GDL at a set point. This lesson shows where. A fifteen-year-old new resident holding a valid permit from another state qualifies only for a Tennessee learner permit. A sixteen-year-old holding a valid out-of-state license issued at least ninety days before applying applies for the Intermediate Restricted License. Between those cases are rules for counting earlier permit time and for checking the out-of-state record before the teen moves up.

lines.text: Fifteen with a permit: Tennessee learner permit.
Need one hundred eighty total permit days.
Must turn sixteen first.

narration.text: A fifteen-year-old new resident holding a valid permit from another state qualifies only for a Tennessee learner permit, and must reach one hundred eighty total days on a permit and turn sixteen before the Intermediate Restricted License. Time on the previous state's permit can count toward the one hundred eighty days if the teen shows a certified driving record issued within the thirty days before the Tennessee application. So bringing a recent certified record can shorten the wait, while arriving without one means counting days only from the Tennessee permit.

lines.text: Any violation or accident: keep the permit.
Until the record meets the less than six points rule.

narration.text: The previous state's record matters. If it shows any violation or accident, the teen keeps a Tennessee learner permit until the Driver Improvement Section confirms the record meets the less than six points rule. That review happens before the teen can advance. A clean record lets the teen move on as soon as the time and age requirements are met. A record with a violation or accident means waiting for that confirmation, even if the teen has already held a permit for long enough in the other state. The record review comes first.

lines.text: Out-of-state license time does not replace it.
Hold Intermediate Restricted one year.

narration.text: Here is the trap for newcomer teens. However long a license was held in another state, the Tennessee Intermediate Restricted License must still be held one year before the Unrestricted level. So a teen who drove on an out-of-state license for two years still spends a year on the Tennessee restricted level. Earlier time can help a teen qualify for the restricted level, but it never replaces the restricted year. Plan for that full year of passenger limits and curfew after arriving, whatever the previous state allowed.

lines.text: Fifteen with an out-of-state permit: which credential?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a fifteen-year-old moves to Tennessee holding a valid learner permit from another state. What can she receive in Tennessee? Work it out before reading on. She qualifies only for a Tennessee learner permit. Before the Intermediate Restricted License, she must reach one hundred eighty total days on a permit and turn sixteen. Her time on the previous state's permit can count toward those days if she shows a certified driving record issued within the thirty days before her Tennessee application. It applies to every newcomer.

lines.text: Fifteen with a permit: permit only.
License over ninety days: Intermediate Restricted.
Under ninety days: clear record and enough days.

narration.text: To close, a fifteen-year-old newcomer with a permit gets a Tennessee learner permit, and earlier permit time counts with a recent certified record. A sixteen-year-old whose out-of-state license is at least ninety days old applies for Intermediate Restricted, while one whose license is under ninety days old needs a clear record showing at least one hundred eighty combined days on a permit or license. Any violation or accident means a record review, and every newcomer still holds the Tennessee restricted license one year before moving up.

why_how.text: An adult must take responsibility for every applicant under eighteen.
School attendance or progress decides whether a teen may drive.
Each added license class, such as a motorcycle, needs its own teen affidavit.

scenario.text: Sam's grandmother wants to sign his teen affidavit because his parents work during the day.

reasoning.text: A grandparent may sign only when authorized by a parent, step-parent, custodian or guardian, and must bring a notarized authorization.

result.text: Sam's grandmother brings a notarized authorization signed by one of his parents.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a report card proves school attendance.

correction.text: Grade cards and school transcripts are never accepted as proof of school attendance or progress.

memory_support.text: Diploma, GED or a fresh form; never a report card.

prompt.text: A teen with a Class D license now wants a motorcycle class. Does the original teen affidavit cover it?

answer.text: No. The parent or guardian must sign a second teenage affidavit for that class.

rationale.text: Each added license class needs its own affidavit.

lines.text: Every applicant under eighteen needs a signer.
The signer accepts financial responsibility.

narration.text: Every applicant under eighteen needs an adult to sign the teen affidavit and cancellation form, joining the application and accepting responsibility, including financial responsibility, for the young driver. This lesson covers who may sign, how the form can be signed when the adult cannot attend, and which school documents prove attendance or progress. It ends with what happens when a student drops out. Each of these rules keeps an adult involved and keeps school connected to the privilege of driving for anyone under eighteen.

lines.text: Parent, foster parent or step-parent at the same address.
Legal guardian.
Authorized grandparent.

narration.text: Allowed signers of the teen affidavit are a parent, foster parent or step-parent sharing the applicant's address, a legal guardian, or a grandparent whom one of those adults has authorized. A grandparent taking on financial responsibility must bring a notarized authorization signed by the parent, step-parent, custodian or guardian. If the adult cannot come to the Driver Service Center, the teen affidavit can be completed ahead of time and signed in front of a notary public. So the signer can be absent, but the signature must still be properly witnessed.

lines.text: Graduates: original diploma or GED.
Enrolled students: original school form.
Form valid thirty days after signing.

narration.text: A graduate proves school status with an original diploma or GED certificate, while an enrolled Tennessee student brings an original school form that is valid for thirty days after the school signs it. Over the summer, a form signed within the last thirty days of the school year is honored until thirty days after the next school year begins. A student at an out-of-state school, or at an approved private or church school without the forms, brings a letter on school letterhead from the principal or headmaster confirming the student is not truant.

lines.text: Grade cards refused.
School transcripts refused.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many families bring a report card or a transcript, assuming it proves the student is in school. Grade cards and school transcripts are never accepted as proof of school attendance or progress. Bring the original diploma or GED certificate, the original school form signed within thirty days, or the principal's letter for out-of-state and private schools. A home-schooled applicant brings a letter from the local director of schools confirming the annual notice of intent to home school, plus a form signed by a parent or guardian.

lines.text: Dropping out costs driving privileges.
First time: returns on going back.
Second time: wait until eighteen.

narration.text: A student fifteen or older who drops out loses driving privileges. After the first dropout, the privilege returns on going back to school, but after a second dropout, the student must wait until eighteen to apply. A student reinstated after returning to school pays a twenty dollars reinstatement fee on top of the application and license fees. So a first dropout is a costly setback, while a second dropout removes the chance to drive until eighteen. Staying in school is part of keeping the license. School and driving go together.

lines.text: Adding a motorcycle class: new affidavit?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a teen who already holds a Class D license wants to add a motorcycle class. Does the original teen affidavit cover the new class? Work it out before reading on. No. A minor adding another license class, such as a motorcycle, needs the parent or guardian to sign a second teenage affidavit for that class. The adult takes on responsibility for each class separately. The usual signer rules still apply, so the second affidavit comes from a parent, legal guardian, step-parent or foster parent at the same address, or an authorized grandparent.

lines.text: Allowed adult signs; notary if absent.
School form within thirty days; no grade cards.
Second dropout: wait until eighteen.

narration.text: To close, an allowed adult signs the teen affidavit and accepts responsibility, including financial responsibility; a grandparent needs a notarized authorization, an absent adult can sign before a notary, and each added class needs a second affidavit. School status is shown with a diploma, a GED, a school form signed within thirty days with a summer extension, or a principal's or home-school letter, never a grade card or transcript. Dropping out costs driving privileges, a reinstatement fee applies, and a second dropout means waiting until eighteen.
